utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case Number IT-02-60-T, The Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Waespi, are there any witnesses this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. No, there is not. We decided not to call this witness who has been anticipated to testify this afternoon. He will be testifying after the summer break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. I'm sorry to hear that. It was our intention to finish the witness list before the summer recess. Could you inform us how many witnesses left in the first group that we should hear after the summer recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I believe without naming the people, there are three witnesses who are left, and we intend to call them as soon as the Court decides to resume the case after the summer break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, we turn to the 94 bis hearing which is about expert reports. On the 17th February, 2003, the Prosecution filed its notice of disclosure of expert witness statements under Rule 94 bis with reports attached. On the 18th February, the Prosecution filed a motion for the admission of witness statements and the prior testimony pursuant to Rule 92 bis. On the 31st of March, 2003, the Defence team of Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Jokic filed their response concerning the 94 bis notice and the 92 bis motion. In their response concerning the 94 bis notice, the Defence team of Mr. Blagojevic accepts the 14 expert reports in lieu of live testimony, and also expresses wishes to cross-examine two expert witnesses. The Defence team for Mr. Jokic accepts 11 expert reports in lieu of live testimony, but also expressed their wishes to cross-examine five expert witnesses. In its response concerning the 92 bis motion, the Defence of Mr. Blagojevic accepts the expert reports or transcripts of the experts' testimony in the Krstic case to be admitted into the evidence in lieu of the oral testimony of the same expert of which it accepts the reports in its response regarding the 94 bis notice. It objects to the admission of the transcript of one expert witness. In its response regarding the 92 bis motion, the Defence team of Mr. Jokic requests the Trial Chamber to deny the 92 bis motion in toto or if the Trial Chamber grants the motion, then all the witnesses will be called for cross-examination. On the 30th May, 2003, the Prosecution filed its notice of disclosure of expert witness statements under Rule 94 bis, providing an updated report of two expert witnesses. On the 30th June, 2003, Mr. Jokic Defence team filed a response accepting the two updated expert reports to be admitted into the evidence without calling the experts to testify in person. The Defence team for Mr. Blagojevic did not file any response. During today's session, this Bench would like to discuss with the parties about those expert reports. First of all, I would like to ask the Prosecution to tell us whether there's any protective measures for any experts during these filings because during the proceedings, their names may be mentioned. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Davis is the expert on our experts.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe there are any protective measures for any of the expert witnesses. We can discuss their names openly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Trial Chamber also observes that both Defence teams object to some of the experts' reports submitted under 94 bis, but did not provide any specific reasons for their objections. So there are some questions we would like to address to both parties. Could I turn to Ms. Sinatra, first. We would like to know why does your team object to the 92 bis response to experts' reports or experts' transcript testimony listed in the Prosecution's 92 bis motion to be admitted while accepting them in lieu of live testimony in its 94 bis response. We found it very strange.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and we're going to change our position on that in the courtroom today. I just wanted to greet you all and for the first time I'm going to take my first shot at saying, Judge Argibay and Judge Vassylenko, I have never had the nerve to try to pronounce your names, but I wanted to go ahead and breakthrough on that, and I'm so happy to be able to address you on this and change our position. We listed 11 expert witnesses that we will allow under 94 bis. And we change our position on the 92 bis, those witnesses' testimony from the Krstic transcript, we have no objections to that also. So that's 11 witnesses that can be admitted from the Krstic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. It was a mystery, Your Honour. Thank you for letting me clear that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And the next question I would like to address to the Defence team of Mr. Blagojevic, Mr. Karnavas, why do you want to cross-examine Mr. Helge Brunborg, and Martin Ols, those two expert witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Mr. President. Thank you for asking me that question. I think -- let me address first Mr. Helge Brunborg. His testimony, I believe, is vital to the Prosecution as well as to the Defence with respect to the issue of genocide, the count of all counts in this particular case. He is a demographer. He testified in the Krstic case, and there are 68 pages of transcript, only six of which were of cross-examination. None of the questions really went into the methodology of the particular report. Mr. Brunborg worked for the OTP as an in-house expert, hardly what one would expect to be an objective outside expert. He was employed by OTP. So while we don't -- we're not suggesting that he's not an expert, I think there is room to suggest that perhaps he is less than objective when it comes to his report. In his initial report, he is rather firm with respect to certain findings. Of course, the centre of the report deals with the actual number of the missing persons. Now, the number -- that particular number obviously is important for a variety of reasons, one for historical; two, for of course all the missing people themselves and their family members, and perhaps even in this particular case, though, I would suggest that you don't necessarily look at a number in particular in order to determine whether genocide has or has not occurred. The percentage is, however, I believe a significant factor. And in his findings, he indicates that perhaps as more than 90 per cent of the people that are missing are from Srebrenica, and then he also says five surrounding municipalities. The -- since then, he prepared an updated report, and in the updated report he is less rigid, if I could put it that way. And perhaps slightly more flexible in his findings. In his -- in that particular report, and we were served of it on 12 April, 2003, paragraph number 1, where it says "Missing by municipality of residence," he states, and I'm just going to read briefly for everyone's convenience, "There is a great uncertainty and debate about the number of people who were in the enclave before it fell on 12 July, 1995. Moreover, it is not known where the people in the enclave came from. Most of them probably, and I underscore myself probably, came from the municipality of Srebrenica itself, but there were also many who came from surrounding municipalities as there were large flows of displaced people in and out of Srebrenica after April 1992 due to armed conflicts in the surrounding areas." And it goes on, and he adjusts the numbers somewhat. And he discusses that issue. Now, this is -- this was provided to us, as I indicated, in April 12th, 2003. Back on 11 July, 1995, there was a letter submitted by Mr. Akashi to the Secretary-General Annan of the United Nations where in it, and this was provided to us by the Prosecution, and for the record, the top number is R008166 -- looks like 2. It's hard to read. But this was provided to us from the Prosecution. It says, on paragraph 2(b) of page 2, it says: "UNHCR reports that 80 to 90 per cent of the population in Srebrenica, (total population is 40.000) are displaced persons who fled fighting earlier in the war, thus they do not have long-standing ties to homes and property in the enclave and will probably be interested in leaving for Tuzla." I mention that because this report was generated by Mr. Akashi. Obviously it was in the hands of the Prosecution. It's dated 11 July, 1995. The gentleman worked for the Office of the Prosecution, I believe, as late as 1997, 1998, all the way to 1999. And obviously, this is a critical issue to the count dealing with genocide. And so, we believe because, one, we have this material before us, we have the UNHCR's prediction that was stated by Mr. Akashi, we have an updated report, which I failed to mention, also took into consideration the NIOD report, the Dutch report, and also the report presented by the government of the Republika Srpska, although I will say that that report in essence is worthless, and I say that for the record and on the record. But he does take into consideration the NIOD report and he does minimise or does -- he takes exception to their findings without going into any great of details. So given all, that given the fact that he wasn't thoroughly cross-examined, given that this is a central issue, we believe that the only way that we can fully satisfy our mandate in representing Mr. Blagojevic, and the only way for the Trial Chamber to fully factor in this important information is to have him here so he can be cross-examined, particularly in light of the fact that he has a new report. So that was the reason why we chose to challenge and to request that Mr. Brunborg come here and be cross-examined. And I want to stress again, he is a Prosecution's paid employee at the time that he makes this report. Hardly someone that I would consider or anyone else would consider, at least from the Defence bar, an objective, qualified expert witness. He may be a qualified expert witness, but objective, that's the part that I take exception to. With respect to the other individual, it was rather perplexing. I believe it's Mr. Martin. He's a forensics expert. From what I was able to glean, and there was precious little of it, I simply could not understand why indeed this particular information was being tendered by the Prosecution. They may have a particular reason. I certainly can't figure it out. And so, before I can sign off on whether I would agree to this report coming in without having the gentleman testify, I need to know a little bit more about it. I don't think that there is a whole lot of dispute as to how the victims were killed in this particular case. The report itself doesn't in any way tend to establish that a particular weapon that belonged to a particular member of the Bratunac Brigade was used, and therefore, there's some kind of nexus, some kind of connection. So I don't fully understand why he's being -- they're bringing him here. Frankly, in my opinion, his testimony or the evidence is not terribly relevant to the issues before this Trial Chamber. And perhaps if I could hear an offer of proof from the Prosecution, I would be more than happy to revisit the issue, and I could do so quickly on my feet. I have I would say a modest amount of expertise in forensic ballistics matters. So if I could hear from the Prosecution, but basically I hope I have answered both of your questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As for the second witness, maybe we could turn to the Prosecutor for asking some questions, because up to now we have no report yet regarding the comparison of the cartridge casings felled from the Drina Corps weapons and the cartridge cases found at various crime scenes. I wonder whether this kind of report will be filed by the Prosecution, or maybe the Prosecution could explain why they would like to call this person to be an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: We would be happy, Your Honour, to revisit this particular report, the Ols report, and to file something in writing if that would be acceptable regarding whether we would continue -- we may be able to drop this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Well, maybe the same question we'll address to Ms. Sinatra. I think you request the cross-examination of five expert witnesses. Would you please tell us why you want them to be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I will need to add to that list and reconsider a few expert witnesses. We just had a meeting with the Office of the Prosecutor at 12.00 today. And we have agreed to revisit five witnesses, and that would be Ten Camp, Fagel, Miljaars, I think, Maloney and Brown. So we are going to be discussing that and try to come to a conclusion on whether those witnesses are necessary. Maloney and Brown, Your Honour, have personal information and have personally dealt with Mr. Jokic, and that's why we really believe that we require that they are present in the courtroom for cross-examination. Post-1995 Dayton Accord, they worked with Mr. Jokic, and the content of their report I have discussed with the Prosecution. We are going to revisit that and we will be discussing the necessity of that report. But those witnesses have personal information dealing with Mr. Jokic, and I think they're relevant and should be called to be cross-examined. As the Court knows, one of the main issues in our case is that Mr. Jokic denies ever being a part of some of the intercepts that the Prosecution attributes to him during July 14th, 1995. Peter French, Robert Greenberg, and another Prosecution witness that I'm adding to my list that I would like to cross-examine is Ms. Stephanie Frease who was their expert witness that they called in the Krstic case. We intend to, if the Prosecution doesn't call them, they will have to be called during the Defence case; that is assuming that at the end of the Prosecutor's case, the Prosecution has met their burden of proof and Mr. Jokic is not acquitted, and we do mount a Defence, then we would be calling these Prosecution witnesses to come and testify, and at that point when they testify, then maybe their reports would be admissible. But until then, since this is one of the major issues in the Defence case, we feel that Mr. French, Mr. Greenberg, and Ms. Frease should appear in the Prosecution's case to be cross-examined. We also have Dean Manning, and I think I should have Mr. Butler on there. But I know that we definitely want to cross-examine Dean Manning who is the author of the report of the Srebrenica investigation and Mr. Butler who has continuing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Ms. Sinatra, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. These two experts have updated versions specifically dealing with the addition of the Zvornik Brigade at this time, and they are very relevant and everything that they have presented to this -- to the OTP that we've read is at issue. Of course, when we filed our response at that time on March 31st, 2003, we were not aware of Patrick Cordingley which we also would need to -- he's not 92 bis. I'm sorry. Those are the only 94 bis experts that we request to appear live in the courtroom for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. To my knowledge, Peter French and Robert Greenberg, both of them have been dropped from the list of the expert witnesses. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think we filed a motion on the 10th of June dropping those, requesting to drop them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And as for that witness, forensic document expert, Mr. Ten Camp, we feel it's very difficult to evaluate the importance of the report because we haven't got any relevant documents in this aspect. Could you give us some explanation on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the three forensic document experts, that's Ten Camp, Fagle, and de Koeijer, all are testifying about the same document, which is Exhibit 905 in the Krstic case. This is a document that relates to the handover of the Drina Corps command. It really relates primarily to Mr. Krstic. I believe those documents -- they may not have been attached in our submission to the Court. I'm not sure. We can check on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But why don't you -- do you need three experts testifying to one document?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I believe that there are issues regarding the stamp impression as well as handwriting and whether there had been any falsification to the document. And each of the experts sort of dealt with a separate aspect of that. As I recall, the reports are each quite brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. Yes, yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just as far as the forensic document analyst from the Krstic case go, I think it's really irrelevant to our case whether Mr. Krstic took over on July 10th or whether he took over on July 20th because the chain of command is not affected in the allegations in our indictment. So I think they're irrelevant actually in the presentation of the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this moment it's difficult for us to rule whether they are relevant or irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: You're correct, we do need more information, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And we noted that in those reports, all the experts, or at least two experts use the words "the possibility," "there is great possibility" which sounds like those experts are not quite sure about certain facts. Maybe that's the way for the experts to deal with something.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I believe that is -- there are sort of varying degrees in the various expert reports of how conclusive the findings are, which is not unusual. The experts generally are applying a range of conclusivity, I suppose it the best way to say it, to their findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we just want some documents, you know, which were analysed by the forensic document experts to be identified for the Trial Chamber and some explanations to be provided regarding their importance.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: We would be happy to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As we understand, we have an additional handwriting expert report. I believe that the Chamber is not in the possession at this moment. Would you please furnish us with that report.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: We have copies here, Your Honour. Would you like them on the Bench now or should we provide them after the hearing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe after the hearing. Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you haven't finished yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Sorry, we intend to file a notice of disclosure under Rule 94 bis as we did with the other experts this afternoon, and we have courtesy copies also of the filing in that form that we can provide in the courtroom today. The actual report has been disclosed already to Defence counsel last Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't know whether the Court would postpone reading the document until we've decided our arguments on admissibility. We will be hiring a document analyst and handwriting expert ourselves. I've contacted them yesterday and faxed them the copies of the documents so that they will be responding and we will have a report very soon also. But is it just admissible because they have completed it, or do they have to call the witness here for cross-examination, and then the report is admissible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at least today, this Bench would not make any decisions in this aspect. We just want to hear from the parties their views and their objections to the admission of those reports. And I believe that if you hired some expert report and you may file your expert report in this aspect if we do not call them as a live witness to testify. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I agree that I would like the opportunity to file my own independent report. But I would also request that Ms. K. Barr be called as a witness in the courtroom. Once her document is analysed by our expert, then we would like to have the opportunity to cross-examine her on her techniques and the facilities that they use and authenticate its reliability or disprove the reliability of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We will bear in mind your comments.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think that's all of our questions from the Bench. Is there anything else that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench? Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would, Your Honour, because in one of our motions we did indicate that we certainly objected to Mr. Butler's findings, both of them or three of them, I believe, and wished to cross-examine him, and I do believe that he intends -- the Prosecution intends to bring him. There is in that particular motion, I also note, that we object to all military expert reports from the Prosecution. But just to be on the safe side, since subsequent to that, we were disclosed with a few pages of question and answer expert report, or whatever you want to call it, from General Cordingley, today we will be filing a motion or just a response so we have a written objection to that particular question and answer statement or report. And of course, we would be delighted to have the General come here so we could hear from him and cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Davis.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I just wanted to respond to a couple of things that have come up. First, there has been some discussion about Mr. Manning, Mr. Butler. They are both live witnesses on the Prosecution's list, so I don't believe there's any dispute as to whether they will be available for cross-examination. The question of the Maloney and Brown report, which is a single report, Ms. Sinatra indicated that we had met prior to this hearing, and in fact we did. And our understanding is that Ms. Sinatra has some interest in questioning these witnesses, or Mr. Maloney anyway, on personal information about Mr. Jokic. And our position on that would be that if the witness needs to be brought here for cross-examination because of the substance of his expert report, that would be appropriate. It sounds to us, and I don't know the details, but it sounds to us as if this is something of an entirely different nature. And if it's not the subject of his expert report, I'm not sure it's appropriate to bring the witness here for cross-examination on those points. We can certainly put the Defence in touch with the witness if they wish to call him as a witness of their own. Finally, on the question of the Brunborg report. As you're aware, we filed a motion under 92 bis for the admission of this report -- I'm sorry, for the prior testimony because we believe it doesn't go directly to the acts and conducts of the accused, as that has been interpreted by the Trial Chambers of this Tribunal. It's of course in the Court's discretion using the factors set forth in 92 bis (A), but we believe one of those factors goes directly to this kind of evidence, and that's (A)(i)(c), which consists of a general or statistical analysis of the ethnic composition, et cetera. It sounds as if Mr. Karnavas wants to address some questions about Mr. Brunborg's qualifications, perhaps bias issues, as well as some issues he raised with respect to his updated report. We wouldn't have any objection to bringing the witness here for cross-examination on those issues, but I believe the initial report is appropriate for admission under 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Sinatra, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted to re-address the issue of Maloney and Brown. It was my understanding at the close of our meeting today that I was going to review those reports and get back to the Prosecutor, and we had not come to a final conclusion on Malone and Brown. And I promise to do that. And I will get back to Ms. Davis on the relevancy of those expert reports. I would also like to express our objections to the form of the semi-pseudo report from General Patrick Cordingley, that has been presented to us, and we ask that the Court order that a more formal expert report be issued and that, of course, it not be admitted in evidence in any form except if the witness will appear in Court to testify. Do I have a couple of other issues to bring up, but should we wait until we finish this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, as for that Maloney and Brown report, how soon could you file your response? Because we have already given you the opportunities, and we hope we could render a decision in this aspect before the summer recess.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the summer recess begins August 1st. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I promise to have a response in the next five days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But in this aspect, you know, I agree with what Ms. Davis says concerning calling these two expert witnesses as live witnesses, to testify on certain factual issues rather than the contents of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to revisit the contents of the report, and we may have an agreement on that if I could just revisit that in the next few days and write a formal response to the Trial Chamber and to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any other matters? Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just wanted a clarification from Ms. Davis, based on what Ms. Davis had indicated. First, I'm not suggesting that Mr. Brunborg is biased simply because he was working for the Prosecution. I'm just saying that he may not be totally objective. That remains to be seen. But from listening to the explanation as to why they wish to bring Mr. Brunborg here to testify would seem to me that it's relevant to the case if indeed it is what she is suggesting, you know, that they merely just want to bring him here for demographic purposes and nothing more. But I dare say, the whole purpose of them bringing him here is to bootstrap his testimony to an argument that they will be making with respect to the charge of genocide, which is what they did in the Krstic case. However, I am very grateful that they agree with our position that he should be brought here. However, there were some qualifications, or at least she seemed to indicate for limited purposes of cross-examination, I think that his entire report is subject to cross-examination, and I think that if the Prosecution does intend to make an argument based on his findings with respect to the issue of genocide, then I think we need a clear answer because obviously that's going to dictate the limitations that you may place upon us with respect to cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any response from Ms. Davis?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: We may well use this report in making our arguments regarding genocide. I don't believe that that takes it out of the realm of 92 bis based on the jurisprudence of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that this report is very important. But it goes to proof of matters other than the acts and conducts of the accused. So I wonder whether there's really a necessity to cross-examine this witness by Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- if we look at the -- if we deconstruct the indictment, they have charged Mr. Blagojevic with a joint criminal enterprise, one of the counts being complicity to commit genocide. Now, if they didn't have that in the indictment, I would agree with you. But he's charged with genocide in essence, or being complicitous to committing genocide. And they are going to need to try to prove that first of all a genocide occurred, or there was complicity to commit genocide, that's step number one; and number two, whether Mr. Blagojevic was a part of that joint criminal enterprise. I think we need to get to step one first, and I think that's where that report comes in. I don't see, if you look at how he was cross-examined in the Krstic trial with, as I said, six pages out of 68, many of the questions not really relevant. And in fact, if you look in one of the pages, I believe it's the second page of the cross-examination, the attorney in that particular case indicated that he did not have all of the material prior to commencing the cross. I do believe it violates Mr. Blagojevic's right to confrontation, especially if the Court, the Trial Chamber, is going to be relying on this particular report in making a decision whether there was genocide or complicity to commit genocide. And I don't think, and -- well, also we have the Prosecution's concession for the first time, I mean, first they danced around the issue. Finally, you know, with asking for a clarification, they come out and tell us the truth, which is, yes, indeed, they intend to use that for their arguments at the end of the trial in asking that you find beyond a reasonable doubt that genocide occurred and Mr. Blagojevic was engaged in complicity to commit genocide. So I think given their admission, and also given their concession, I should say, that Mr. Helge Brunborg should come here and testify, I think that in all fairness to the Defence, that we should hear from him because otherwise I will have to -- I can only challenge him by bringing in my own expert. And it would be very difficult to have one expert just challenge a cold transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, you have to understand that to prove genocide, you need a lot of preconditions. The specific number of the population, the reduce of the percentage of the components of the population in such an area is not necessarily implies there's a genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But I agree with you that it's an important report, and we'll study it very carefully, and we'll make our decision at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And also please keep in mind that he was an employee of the Office of the Prosecution. I think that does have some significance as opposed to being, you know, someone from an independent source. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I don't think, you know, it is in the rule there's a qualification for the expert witness. It's not like in other jurisdictions, you know, to be an expert, you should be purely objective and should have nothing to do with both parties, with the incident. That's in some jurisdictions. But here, you know, in our Rules of Procedure, there's no specific article regulating the qualification of an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree with you, Your Honour. And even in other jurisdictions, you can have somebody who is employed by the Prosecution or the police coming as an expert. But I do believe that no matter where you go, including The Hague, one factor for the Court to consider is perhaps bias on the part of the witness because he's employed, and of course since he is employed by the very same institution that is trying to achieve a particular goal, it may be "may," and I don't say that there will be, but there may be some instances where they may fudge on certain facts. I'm not suggesting that that is the case here, and it would be unfair for me to do so simply by reading his report or his testimony. I do, however, believe that that is an area that is necessary for the Defence to probe because after all, the finders of the fact need to make a decision as to the objectivity of the individual. I mean, Butler is a good example. He works for the Prosecution for five years, six, or whatever. Hardly what I would consider somebody who's objective especially when he's out there day in and day out with the Prosecutors, meeting the witnesses, having lunch with the prosecutors, spending weekends with the prosecutors, travelling together. Sooner or later you begin to lose that objectivity. And I'm not suggesting that the report itself may not be objective, but I think it calls into the question the objectivity and it's an area proper for the Defence to probe and for obviously the Trial Chamber to consider in factoring what weight, if any, if any, to give the report and/or the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, you have to remember that your theory is also equally applied to your expert witness in your case in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, I do. So I say this knowing that what is good for the Prosecution is good for the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, are we completed with the 94 bis discussion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think so, unless you have any other matters to bring up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I don't know if this is considered a Status Conference, but I would like to bring up two other matters that I think are pressing on the Defence of Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And just expending further on Mr. Karnavas's arguments on experts and having to call our own, we do have a problem. The Registry has approved 100 hours total for all experts that come to testify for the Defence. And as you can see by the mammoth amount of Prosecution experts that are coming, the five, six, seven years they have spent with their expert witnesses, being able to prepare their case, and we've hired one expert so far, and he has used 70 hours. That leaves 30 hours if we want to hire a handwriting expert, if we want to hire a military expert, if we want to hire anybody to contest or analyse the expert reports of the Prosecution. We do not have enough facilities. We don't have enough hours. We don't have any money to do so. And I don't know how we're going to try to justify this under Article 20 and 21, that equality of arms which I know you're all tired of hearing about. But since they have spent 50.000 hours on their experts, and we are only allowed a hundred hours total, I think there has been some input from the Trial Chamber because the Registry has made a decision, and I can't take it any further without any assistance from the Trial Chamber at this point. So that's one of the issues I have to raise. I doubt if the Prosecution has any input into this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: We don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And may I request assistance from the Trial Chamber in dealing with this and assisting us in getting more facilities, more hours, in order to hire our expert witnesses. I contacted one yesterday, a handwriting expert, but I only have 30 hours left for our whole Defence team. And my intercept and linguistic expert isn't completed yet. So we're really at a disadvantage at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, you know, not unlike any other domestic jurisdictions, the Registrar is an independent branch of this Tribunal. We cannot order the Registrar to do anything. We only could convey your comments and observations to the attention of the Registrar and ask them to do whatever possible to help you to get out of that situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking for. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This is all we could do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: That's the best that I could ask for right now, and I would appreciate any assistance that the Trial Chamber could give us at this time in the way of a recommendation or an opinion. And then I have one other matter to bring up. That is the LiveNote. The Prosecution has LiveNote. The Chambers have LiveNote. The team of Blagojevic have LiveNote. But the team of Jokic has been denied access to the LiveNote programme. So when everybody can cut and paste from a record into documents, we don't have that ability. I have requested LiveNote. They said that they have made a recent decision that it's not given to Defence counsel any more. I don't know how we can overcome this disadvantage in the middle of trial right now. But because everybody in the courtroom has access to LiveNote except this team, I think it puts us at an excessive disadvantage at this point. I'm only asking the Court one more time for an opinion or a recommendation, or even an order that we all be able to place our documents in here and take our records home and cut and paste from them. We don't have the programme installed on our computers to be able to utilise these computers that are provided for us during trial in the courtroom. So it's another Status Conference issue that I would like to have some input from the Trial Chamber on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think you are not the only one who does not have the LiveNote. I myself don't have the LiveNote. And right from the start of this case, that is 14th of May, I made several requests to install the LiveNote on my computer. But up to now, I haven't got any. But do you get hard copies of the transcript the next morning?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: It's not the next morning. It's five or six days later before we get the hard copy in our box. But the disadvantage is that the other people can cut and paste from a document and put it into -- I'm sorry if I have insulted the Registry in any way. I think that we have -- they're much more current than that. But it's too late in order to respond like the next day if we wanted to file something, we don't have the ability to cut and paste from the LiveNote. And you know, if we have to sit and type everything out once more from a hard copy, it puts us at a disadvantage again. I want to express to the Trial Chamber, I'm very sorry that you don't have access to the programme either. And I do hope that when you make your request, that you sign our name at the bottom also. If you could assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, my practice is I have it copied on a hard disk and I bring it back to my office to look at it. But certainly we will convey your complaints to the Registrar and ask them to solve this problem as soon as possible, including mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I wish you the best of luck and thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any other matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Nothing further from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. The last matter is about the resume of the hearings. As we mentioned before that after the first group of the witnesses, we will hear some substantive, material witnesses, including Mr. Obrenovic and Mr. Nikolic. So we believe that before the counsel issue for Mr. Blagojevic is finally settled, it is very unsafe for us to proceed on those substantive witnesses. So we decided to have a break until after the summer recess. We'll resume somewhere in the middle of September. If the decision is rendered by the Appeals Chamber on the counsel issue, we might hear some substantive witnesses. And if not, we'll continue to hear the three witnesses left before the summer recess. This Trial Chamber will issue a scheduling order at the beginning of the next week so that everybody will be informed on the re-opening date of this hearing. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just one point for clarification, you only want to hear the three remaining witnesses, or also Mr. Obrenovic and Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it depends whether we have received the decisions by the Appeals Chamber rendered by the appeal. So at this moment, it's very difficult for us to predict how soon that decision will be rendered by the Appeals Chamber. We understand there will be three weeks of summer recess and only after the summer recess that the appeal could be entertained by the Appeals Chamber. So we could only make a tentative scheduling order. We'll begin the hearing somewhere in the middle of September. If we have a decision, there's a possibility we hear some more substantive witnesses. If we don't have that decision, we'll continue to exhaust the witness list in the first group of witnesses. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have visited with the Prosecution about this issue, and I think I've mentioned it in Court before, that it will be very difficult for us to be prepared for Mr. Obrenovic before October. He is the most important witness that the Prosecution is bringing to testify with evidence that would be damaging to Mr. Jokic. Even if there is a decision by mid-September, we would like to request the Court to hear the other witnesses first to allow us more time to prepare for Mr. Obrenovic. That may put his testimony for us -- may be solved, and he may not come until October at that point. But instead of if there's a decision, putting him on the stand when there are other witnesses that could be heard and give the Defence a chance for preparation for this witness, we would request that the remaining witnesses on the list from pre-summer break be heard first, and that Mr. Obrenovic be heard after these witnesses are completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. Obrenovic pled guilty in May. And in September, there will be three or four months that the Defence team of Mr. Jokic knows that he will be a witness to testify against your client. I believe that that period of time is enough for you to prepare the cross-examination to that very important witness from the Prosecution. But anyway, if you have any suggestions, you are free to file written submissions, and we'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I do understand that it appears to be sufficient time to prepare. But when you're in trial and you're preparing for each witness each day, it takes away from the time that you have to spend on the most important witness. And now that we're having a break, we can begin that preparation properly. I just ask the Court not to put the rights of the accused on the same level, Mr. Jokic being presumed is not, on the same level with a man who has pled guilty and just wants to be sentenced because you can't compare the issues here. Mr. Jokic is presumed innocent, and I'd like for -- I'm just asking the Court to please put the other witnesses before Mr. Obrenovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, I think that's all for this hearing. We're adjourned until middle of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: at 3.16 p.m. Sine die. 24 25
